targets.title: Tor: The Second-Generation Onion Router
targets.authors: Roger Dingledine, Nick Mathewson, Paul F. Syverson
targets.why_needed: The onion-routing construction (per-relay layered encryption, no single relay holding both origin and destination) that every tier-1 anonymity mechanism in this domain assumes or compares against. Need the original design rationale and the three-relay circuit parameter, not a secondary description.

targets.title: Mixminion: Design of a Type III Anonymous Remailer Protocol
targets.authors: George Danezis, Roger Dingledine, Nick Mathewson
targets.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
targets.why_needed: The mix-network design the brief names for message-based (store-and-forward) anonymity, predating and structurally distinct from the continuous-traffic Poisson-mixing line (Loopix). Needed for a from-first-principles comparison of mix-network families, not an assumed superiority of one.

targets.title: Private Information Retrieval
targets.authors: Benny Chor, Oded Goldreich, Eyal Kushilevitz, Madhu Sudan
targets.why_needed: Defines PIR itself and the multi-server (information-theoretic, non-colluding-server) construction that every single-server lattice-based PIR paper in this list positions itself against. Need the original communication-complexity bounds for k-server PIR, derived from first principles rather than assumed.

targets.title: Software Protection and Simulation on Oblivious RAMs
targets.authors: Oded Goldreich, Rafail Ostrovsky
targets.why_needed: Defines Oblivious RAM and proves the original bandwidth-multiplier lower bound the brief asks about; every later ORAM construction (Path ORAM, etc.) states its overhead against this bound. Needed to state the multiplier as a derived quantity rather than a recalled folk number.

targets.title: Distributed Point Functions and Their Applications
targets.authors: Niv Gilboa, Yuval Ishai
targets.why_needed: Introduces the distributed point function (DPF) primitive underlying every multi-server PIR and PIR-based metadata-private-messaging scheme in this list (Talek, Pung's successors, Express). Need the construction and its key-size/communication bound, since the brief explicitly asks for DPF-based multi-server PIR.

targets.title: Deep Fingerprinting: Undermining Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Deep Learning
targets.authors: Payap Sirinam, Mohsen Imani, Marc Juarez, Matthew Wright
targets.why_needed: The deep-learning classifier that the prior pass's headline numbers (98% vs undefended, 90%+ vs WTF-PAD, reduced to 49.7% by Walkie-Talkie) are attributed to. Every one of those figures must be re-derived from this paper's own tables, with dataset size, closed/open-world setting, and number of monitored sites stated — the prior-pass error pattern applies directly here.

targets.title: Toward an Efficient Website Fingerprinting Defense
targets.authors: Marc Juarez, Mohsen Imani, Mike Perry, Claudia Diaz, Matthew Wright
targets.why_needed: The WTF-PAD defense paper itself. The prior pass cites its overhead as a range (32-54%) without stating which experimental condition each end of the range corresponds to; that must come from this paper's own measurement tables, not a repeated range.

targets.title: Effective Attacks and Provable Defenses for Website Fingerprinting
targets.authors: Tao Wang, Xiang Cai, Rishab Nithyanand, Rob Johnson, Ian Goldberg
targets.why_needed: This is the Walkie-Talkie paper, cited in the prior pass and the brief by that name only; need the actual title and the paper's own reported classifier-accuracy-under-defense figure and its overhead, since 'Walkie-Talkie' is a name, not a citation.

targets.title: A Systematic Approach to Developing and Evaluating Website Fingerprinting Defenses
targets.authors: Xiang Cai, Rishab Nithyanand, Tao Wang, Rob Johnson, Ian Goldberg
targets.why_needed: This is the Tamaraw paper (constant-rate padding, named in the brief by mechanism name only). Need the actual per-direction rate and burst-alignment parameters and the measured bandwidth overhead against the closed-world classifier used, as a fixed-rate padding baseline against which later adaptive defenses (RegulaTor, Surakav, FRONT) state their improvement.

targets.title: Zero-delay Lightweight Defenses against Website Fingerprinting
targets.authors: Jiajun Gong, Tao Wang
targets.why_needed: This is the FRONT defense (front-loaded padding). Need its own measured overhead-versus-classifier-accuracy tradeoff curve, since the brief lists it as a distinct 2020 defense to compare against Walkie-Talkie's 2014 numbers and the 2022-2024 defenses below.

targets.title: RegulaTor: A Straightforward Website Fingerprinting Defense
targets.authors: James K. Holland, Nicholas Hopper
targets.why_needed: A 2022 defense the prior pass never mentions. Its own paper reports overhead-versus-defended-accuracy figures against Deep Fingerprinting, WTF-PAD, and FRONT on a common dataset; those numbers are the currency check the brief requires for a field that 'moved fast.'

targets.title: Surakav: Generating Realistic Traces for a Strong Website Fingerprinting Defense
targets.authors: Jiajun Gong, Wuqi Zhang, Charles Zhang, Tao Wang
targets.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
targets.why_needed: A GAN-based trace-generation defense, competing directly with FRONT (same lead author, later paper) and RegulaTor. Need its measured accuracy-versus-overhead numbers against Deep Fingerprinting to place it correctly relative to the others on the same axis.

targets.title: Real-Time Website Fingerprinting Defense via Traffic Cluster Anonymization
targets.authors: Meng Shen, Kexin Ji, Jinhe Wu, Qi Li, Xiangdong Kong, Ke Xu, Liehuang Zhu
targets.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
targets.why_needed: A 2024 defense at the top security venue, satisfying the brief's explicit requirement for 2023-2026 website-fingerprinting defenses. Need its measured latency overhead (the paper's 'real-time' and 'zero-delay' claims recur across this literature and must be checked against each paper's own definition of delay).

targets.title: Countmamba: A Generalized Website Fingerprinting Attack via Coarse-Grained Representation and Fine-Grained Prediction
targets.authors: Xianwen Deng, Ruijie Zhao, Yanhao Wang, Mingwei Zhan, Zhi Xue, Yijun Wang
targets.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
targets.why_needed: A 2025 attack, satisfying the brief's explicit requirement to include 2024-2026 work rather than treating Deep Fingerprinting (2018) as the current state of the art. Need to check whether its reported accuracy against the current defenses (RegulaTor, Surakav, FRONT) supersedes the 2018-2020 attack-defense numbers the prior pass relied on.

targets.title: The Loopix Anonymity System
targets.authors: Ania M. Piotrowska, Jamie Hayes, Tariq Elahi, Sebastian Meiser, George Danezis
targets.why_needed: The Poisson-mixing, per-hop independent-exponential-delay design that Nym deploys. Need the paper's own throughput-per-relay and end-to-end latency distribution (not a single summary number) and the exact loop-cover-traffic rate parameter, since the prior pass's 'upward of 300 messages per second... under 1.5 ms' figures must be checked against the paper's stated experimental topology.

targets.title: Vuvuzela: Scalable Private Messaging Resistant to Traffic Analysis
targets.authors: Jelle van den Hooff, David Lazar, Matei Zaharia, Nickolai Zeldovich
targets.why_needed: The differential-privacy-noise mixing design that the Stadium/Karaoke/Yodel line (same MIT group, successive papers) each state their improvement against. Need Vuvuzela's own measured latency and per-server dead-drop throughput as the baseline those later papers compare to.

targets.title: Stadium: A Distributed Metadata-Private Messaging System
targets.authors: Nirvan Tyagi, Yossi Gilad, Derek Leung, Matei Zaharia, Nickolai Zeldovich
targets.why_needed: States itself as scaling Vuvuzela's single-server-pair design to many servers via verifiable shuffling. Need its own measured throughput scaling with server count, and the exact security assumption (number of honest servers required) it needs, which differs from Vuvuzela's two-server assumption.

targets.title: Karaoke: Distributed Private Messaging Immune to Passive Traffic Analysis
targets.authors: David Lazar, Yossi Gilad, Nickolai Zeldovich
targets.why_needed: States a latency improvement over Vuvuzela and Stadium by batching multiple rounds together; need the paper's own measured latency-versus-user-count curve to check whether that improvement is asymptotic or a constant-factor result tied to a specific deployment size.

targets.title: Yodel: Strong Metadata Security for Voice Calls
targets.authors: David Lazar, Yossi Gilad, Nickolai Zeldovich
targets.why_needed: Same group's follow-on to Karaoke, targeting voice-call latency budgets (tens of milliseconds) rather than message latency (seconds). Need its own round-trip latency figure to determine whether any mix-network construction in this line meets an interactive-latency bar, directly relevant to the brief's open 'private search at interactive latency' question, generalized to interactive communication.

targets.title: Talek: Private Group Messaging with Hidden Access Patterns
targets.authors: Raymond Cheng, William Scott, Elisaweta Masserova, Irene Zhang, Vipul Goyal, Thomas E. Anderson, Arvind Krishnamurthy, Bryan Parno
targets.why_needed: A PIR-based (not mix-based) approach to hiding who-reads-what in group messaging, giving a distinct point of comparison against the differential-privacy-noise family (Vuvuzela/Stadium/Karaoke/Yodel). Need its measured per-message server computation cost to compare directly against the PIR throughput figures in this same domain.

targets.title: Studying the Anonymity Trilemma with a Discrete-event Mix Network Simulator
targets.authors: Ania M. Piotrowska
targets.why_needed: An independent, simulator-based empirical comparison of three deployed mix networks (Elixxir, HOPR, Nym) against the trilemma bound, by the original Loopix author. This is the paper to cite for Nym's actual deployed anonymity/latency/bandwidth tradeoff, since Nym itself has no peer-reviewed measurement paper (Nym's public materials are project documentation, not primary evidence per rule 1).

targets.title: PIR with Compressed Queries and Amortized Query Processing
targets.authors: Sebastian Angel, Hao Chen, Kim Laine, Srinath T. V. Setty
targets.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
targets.why_needed: This is the SealPIR paper. The prior pass states its throughput as '102 MB/s' with no experimental condition attached; need the paper's own hardware description, database size, and single- versus multi-thread setting, since the brief flags this whole area as one where 'the prior pass's numbers are likely stale.'

targets.title: OnionPIR: Response Efficient Single-Server PIR
targets.authors: Muhammad Haris Mughees, Hao Chen, Ling Ren
targets.why_needed: States an improvement over SealPIR specifically in response size (the client-side download), a different axis than server throughput. Need the paper's own response-size-versus-database-size table to compare against Spiral's response size on the same axis.

targets.title: Spiral: Fast, High-Rate Single-Server PIR via FHE Composition
targets.authors: Samir Jordan Menon, David J. Wu
targets.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
targets.why_needed: The prior pass's tier-3 selection at '310 MB/s, 14 kB query, 84 kB response, 24.5 s server computation on a 7.9 GB database.' Full text confirmed retrievable (spot-checked: 46 pages at eprint.iacr.org/2022/368.pdf) and states exactly this scenario; next-pass extraction must pull the full table across database sizes, not only the headline row, and must check that table against SimplePIR/DoublePIR's throughput on the same database sizes.

targets.title: One Server for the Price of Two: Simple and Fast Single-Server Private Information Retrieval
targets.authors: Alexandra Henzinger, Matthew M. Hong, Henry Corrigan-Gibbs, Sarah Meiklejohn, Vinod Vaikuntanathan
targets.why_needed: This single paper defines both SimplePIR and DoublePIR, named in the brief as separate systems; need the actual relationship (DoublePIR trades some of SimplePIR's throughput for a much smaller client-held hint) and the paper's own throughput numbers, since the prior pass says only 'SimplePIR reaches higher throughput and requires the client to download a large precomputed hint first' without a number for either the throughput or the hint size.

targets.title: Piano: Extremely Simple, Single-Server PIR with Sublinear Server Computation
targets.authors: Mingxun Zhou, Andrew Park, Wenting Zheng, Elaine Shi
targets.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
targets.why_needed: Claims sublinear (rather than linear) server computation per query after preprocessing, which if it holds directly attacks the brief's open problem 4 ('current single-server PIR costs seconds per query on multi-gigabyte databases'). Need the paper's own per-query server-time figure after amortized preprocessing, and the preprocessing cost it is amortized against, since a sublinear-per-query claim with an expensive un-amortized preprocessing step is a different claim from true interactive-latency PIR.

targets.title: YPIR: High-Throughput Single-Server PIR with Silent Preprocessing
targets.authors: Samir Jordan Menon, David J. Wu
targets.why_needed: A 2024 follow-on to Spiral by the same authors, explicitly named by the brief's '2023-2026 PIR result' requirement. 'Silent preprocessing' is a specific claim (no interaction needed to generate preprocessing material) that must be checked against what SimplePIR/DoublePIR's 'hint download' actually requires, since the two papers may be making incompatible claims about what round trip is eliminated.

targets.title: FrodoPIR: Simple, Scalable, Single-Server Private Information Retrieval
targets.authors: Alex Davidson, Goncalo Pestana, Sofia Celi
targets.why_needed: A 2023 single-server PIR result built on plain LWE rather than ring-LWE (unlike Spiral/OnionPIR), trading response size for a simpler security assumption. Need its own throughput and per-client preprocessed-database-size figures to place on the same axis as SimplePIR/Piano/YPIR.

targets.title: Efficient Batched Oblivious PRF with Applications to Private Set Intersection
targets.authors: Vladimir Kolesnikov, Ranjit Kumaresan, Mike Rosulek, Ni Trieu
targets.why_needed: The OPRF-based PSI construction (commonly cited as KKRT) that the prior pass's own SPLiNTERNET-integration document names as 'the fix path' for replacing salted-hash PSI. Need this paper's own measured per-element cost and total running time at a stated set size, since it is being relied on as an actual replacement mechanism, not only a name.

targets.title: Private Set Intersection in the Internet Setting From Lightweight Oblivious PRF
targets.authors: Melissa Chase, Peihan Miao
targets.why_needed: States an improvement over KKRT specifically for the unbalanced, high-latency-network setting (one large set on a server, one small set from a client) which is the relevant setting for a client querying a network peer, as opposed to KKRT's original two-comparable-sized-set, low-latency LAN setting. Need its own measured communication and running-time figures at the set-size asymmetry it targets.

targets.title: Access Pattern disclosure on Searchable Encryption: Ramification, Attack and Mitigation
targets.authors: Mohammad Saiful Islam, Mehmet Kuzu, Murat Kantarcioglu
targets.why_needed: The first of the three SSE leakage-abuse attack papers the brief names by author surname only. Need the actual attack mechanism (co-occurrence pattern matching against a known-plaintext reference distribution) and its stated auxiliary-knowledge requirement, to state precisely what SSE reveals beyond 'match/no-match.'

targets.title: Leakage-Abuse Attacks Against Searchable Encryption
targets.authors: David Cash, Paul Grubbs, Jason Perry, Thomas Ristenpart
targets.why_needed: The second of the three named leakage-abuse attacks, generalizing Islam-Kuzu-Kantarcioglu to a wider class of SSE schemes and a formal leakage-profile framework. Need the paper's own count-attack and file-injection-attack success rates at stated auxiliary-knowledge fractions.

targets.title: Learning to Reconstruct: Statistical Learning Theory and Encrypted Database Attacks
targets.authors: Paul Grubbs, Marie-Sarah Lacharite, Brice Minaud, Kenneth G. Paterson
targets.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
targets.why_needed: The third named leakage-abuse attack, reframing query and value reconstruction as a statistical learning problem to give reconstruction guarantees under weaker assumptions than the two prior attacks. Need its stated bound on the auxiliary-distribution assumption strength required, which determines how easy the attack is against a realistic peer holding real-world data.

targets.title: Path ORAM: An Extremely Simple Oblivious RAM Protocol
targets.authors: Emil Stefanov, Marten van Dijk, Elaine Shi, Christopher W. Fletcher, Ling Ren, Xiangyao Yu, Srinivas Devadas
targets.why_needed: The ORAM construction actually deployed in practice and cited as the reference point for 'the bandwidth multiplier' the prior pass states as 10-100x with no derivation. Need the paper's own asymptotic bandwidth blowup formula (as a function of the client-side stash size and tree depth) so that figure is derived rather than recalled.

targets.title: Yes, There is an Oblivious RAM Lower Bound!
targets.authors: Kasper Green Larsen, Jesper Buus Nielsen
targets.why_needed: Proves an Omega(log n) bandwidth-overhead lower bound for statistically secure ORAM, closing a gap left open by earlier work that only had lower bounds for restricted ORAM classes. This is the structural ceiling against which any claimed low-overhead ORAM construction must be checked, directly relevant to whether the brief's ORAM bandwidth multiplier can ever be reduced below a logarithmic factor.

targets.title: Dissent: Accountable Anonymous Group Messaging
targets.authors: Henry Corrigan-Gibbs, Bryan Ford
targets.why_needed: The dining-cryptographers-network (DC-net) based anonymous-broadcast system the brief names first. Need its own measured per-round latency and message throughput as a function of group size, since the brief states DC-net coordination cost 'grows with group size' as an unquantified claim from the prior pass that must be replaced with the paper's actual scaling figure.

targets.title: Herbivore: A Scalable and Efficient Protocol for Anonymous Communication
targets.authors: Sharad Goel, Mark Robson, Milo Polte, Emin Gun Sirer
targets.venue: Cornell University Computer Science Technical Report 2003-1890
targets.why_needed: Not indexed on DBLP or Crossref (confirmed absent from both; it is a technical report, not a peer-reviewed venue publication), but institutionally archived at Cornell eCommons. Its clique-partitioning approach to DC-nets (fixed clique size k, 3k-user cap per clique) is the scaling mechanism named alongside Dissent and Riposte in the brief and needs its own measured bandwidth/latency figures at a stated clique size.

targets.title: Riposte: An Anonymous Messaging System Handling Millions of Users
targets.authors: Henry Corrigan-Gibbs, Dan Boneh, David Mazieres
targets.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
targets.why_needed: States an improvement over Dissent/Herbivore-style DC-nets by using a write-only PIR-like scheme (distributed point functions again, connecting back to Gilboa-Ishai) instead of pairwise DC-net coordination, claiming the 'millions of users' scale in its title. Need the paper's own measured server-side computation and bandwidth cost per round at a stated user count, to check that scaling claim against Dissent's group-size-dependent cost.
